title: The county clerk who named a valley

place.label: Hayes Street between Van Ness Avenue and Franklin Street

hook: Hayes Valley is named for a Gold Rush county clerk whose brother helped name the streets and who also held the franchise for the West Coast's first railway.
story: Before there was a Hayes Valley there was Colonel Thomas Hayes, San Francisco's county clerk from 1853 to 1856. He held a large tract of land out here in the Western Addition, then the city's western fringe. The Van Ness Ordinance confirmed his claim, and his own house stood on Hayes Street between Van Ness and Franklin [1]. In 1856 a three-man committee named the streets of the new district. One of its members was Hayes's brother Michael, who, according to the Museum of the City of San Francisco, 'probably was instrumental' in giving this street the family name [1]. Hayes also held the franchise, granted by the state Legislature, for the Market Street Railway. It was developed by François Pioche, a Paris-born importer and banker, and it became the first railway on the Pacific Coast [2]. The company was founded in 1857. Market Street was graded, and three years later the first car rolled out toward 16th and Valencia streets, pulled by steam 'dummies' and later by horses [2]. Hayes's house is long gone. Its block is now part of the Civic Center's performing-arts district, but his name runs west across the whole neighbourhood.

title: Orphans, refugees and a teachers' college

place.label: Former San Francisco Orphan Asylum block (Haight, Buchanan, Hermann and Laguna streets)

hook: For $100, a group of women bought two remote blocks for their orphans. The site went on to shelter 1906 refugees and a teachers' college.
story: The San Francisco Orphan Asylum Society was founded in 1851 by women who met at the home of the Reverend Albert Williams, to care for siblings orphaned by cholera on the way to California. By 1852 it had outgrown its first home [1]. For $100 its managers bought two blocks bounded by Haight, Buchanan, Hermann and Laguna. The land was then thought remote, far beyond the city limits [1]. On March 22, 1854, the children moved into a two-storey stone dormitory, with stone hauled free by the Spring Valley Water Company [1]. It grew to about 300 children, and donors included Levi Strauss, Adolph Sutro and Lillie Coit. Local legend says Haight and Waller streets are named for two of its board members [1]. The 1906 earthquake damaged the building but did not destroy it, and refugees camped on the slopes nearby [1]. The Society had leased the southern half of its land to the state for the San Francisco State Normal School, which lost its Powell Street building and all its records in the fire. Within ten days, president Frederic Burk had found a new site 'on upper Market Street'. Classes resumed that June, making it the first public school in the city to reopen [2][1]. The orphans left in 1919, and the state bought the property [1].

title: The breakfast that burned Hayes Valley

place.label: South side of Hayes Street just east of Gough Street

hook: A woman cooked breakfast on a stove with an earthquake-cracked chimney. The fire that started there burned a church, a college and most of Hayes Valley east of Octavia.
story: At about 9 a.m. on April 18, 1906, in a house on the south side of Hayes Street about 75 feet east of Gough, a woman lit her stove to cook breakfast. The earthquake had damaged her chimney, and fire broke out [1]. With every fire company already busy, nobody could stop what became known as the 'ham and egg fire'. The historian Lawrence Kennedy judged that it 'burned over more territory than any other single fire' [1]. By about 1 p.m. it had reached the St. Nicholas Hotel at Market and Hayes. St. Ignatius Church and College at Van Ness and Hayes was burning, and flying embers set the roof of Mechanics' Pavilion alight [1]. The Jesuit church had been built in 1880 and could hold 4,000 worshippers. It was destroyed along with its college [2]. Through the night the fire spread west and north. Soldiers ordered the Lagan family out of their Haight Street home at 2 a.m. [3]. At about 5 a.m. on April 19, the fire was finally stopped along Octavia Street, 'assisted by neither wind, hills, or vacant lots', and Octavia became a permanent edge of the burned district [1]. At Market and Octavia, the 1894 Fallon Building is the only survivor of its row. The buildings to its east burned [4].

title: Rube Goldberg's building for his father

place.label: R. L. Goldberg Building, 182-198 Gough Street

hook: The cartoonist whose name means 'needlessly complicated' built something quite simple on Gough Street: shops downstairs and a flat for his widowed dad upstairs.
story: Before his name became shorthand for absurdly complicated contraptions, Reuben Goldberg was a San Francisco boy, born here in 1883. His father, a city police and fire commissioner, steered him toward engineering. Rube graduated from UC Berkeley in 1904 and went to work as an engineer for the city's Water and Sewers Department [2]. He lasted six months, then quit to become a sports cartoonist at the San Francisco Chronicle [2]. In 1911 he commissioned a building at 182–198 Gough Street. Its ground-floor shops brought in rent, and upstairs were two apartments, one for himself and one for his widowed father, Max [1][2]. Goldberg spent most of his career in New York, where his drawings of machines that did simple jobs in hilariously roundabout ways made him famous. He won the Pulitzer Prize for political cartooning in 1948 [2]. He still made long visits to his San Francisco home and kept the building for the rest of his life [1]. The city later made it Landmark No. 268 for its close association with the man whose name now describes any device 'deliberately over-engineered to perform a simple task' [1].

title: A war memorial that sings

place.label: War Memorial Opera House, 301 Van Ness Avenue

hook: A court ruling blocked San Francisco's opera house until a returning major had an idea: build it as a memorial to the war dead.
story: The 1906 fire destroyed San Francisco's theatres and opera houses. In 1911 and 1912 the Musical Association tried to build a new hall, but the state Supreme Court ruled that the city could not give land for what was essentially a private building [1]. The group met again in April 1918. That November Major Charles H. Kendrick came home from the First World War with an idea: combine the hall with a memorial to the war's veterans [1]. The Association bought land on Van Ness Avenue, where St. Ignatius Church and College had stood before 1906 [1]. Arthur Brown Jr. and G. Albert Lansburgh designed twin buildings, an Opera House and a Veterans Building, facing City Hall [1]. Foundation work began on January 28, 1931, and the cornerstones were laid on Armistice Day that year [1][2]. The Opera House opened on October 15, 1932, in the depths of the Depression, with Puccini's Tosca. Gaetano Merola conducted and Claudia Muzio sang the title role [1][2]. The nine performances sold out, and three more were added [2]. According to the city's landmark report, it was the first municipally owned opera house in the world [1].

title: Fifty nations sign on Van Ness

place.label: Veterans Building and Herbst Theatre, 401 Van Ness Avenue

hook: In the spring of 1945 the world came to Van Ness Avenue. Delegates of fifty nations spent two months there writing the United Nations Charter.
story: From April 25 to June 26, 1945, while the Second World War was still being fought, delegates of fifty nations met in San Francisco to write the Charter of the United Nations. There were 850 delegates, 3,500 people once advisers and staff were counted, and more than 2,500 press, radio and newsreel reporters and observers [1]. The twin War Memorial buildings on Van Ness were the conference's home. According to the UN, the Charter was adopted unanimously in the Opera House on June 25. The next day it was signed in the auditorium of the Veterans Building, now the Herbst Theatre [1]. The War Memorial's own history agrees, with President Truman and other dignitaries signing on the Veterans Auditorium stage [2]. The city's 1974 landmark resolution, however, puts the signing 'on the great stage of the Opera House' [3]. Six years later the Opera House hosted another ending. On September 8, 1951, the peace treaty with Japan was signed on its stage. The War Memorial calls the broadcast America's first live coast-to-coast television broadcast [2].

title: The money fortress on Clinton Mound
hook: After 1906, refugees camped on this rocky hill. Since 1937 it has held a working U.S. Mint that almost nobody is allowed to visit.
story: The rocky rise above Market and Duboce was once known as Clinton Mound. After the 1906 earthquake and fire, refugees camped on its slopes [1]. In 1937 the federal government built the third home of the San Francisco Mint on the hill. The branch had opened in 1854 to serve the Gold Rush mines [2]. Designed by Gilbert Stanley Underwood in a stripped classical style, the building at 155 Hermann Street replaced the 1874 'Old Mint' on Fifth Street, which had saved the nation's gold reserves from the 1906 fire [2][3]. Since then its history has been oddly stop-start. From 1955, circulating coinage was suspended for 13 years, and from 1962 to 1988 the building was officially only an 'assay office' [2]. Since 1975 it has struck almost nothing but proof coins for collectors, apart from Susan B. Anthony dollars and some cents, many marked with a small 'S' [2]. Visitors are admitted only as a rare exception. For the Mint's 50th anniversary in May 1987, a limited number of people got a tour, advertised in the Chronicle with reservations required [2]. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1988 [2][3].

title: The freeway Hayes Valley finally beat
hook: Planners called the neighbourhood blighted and ran a double-decker freeway through it. After an earthquake and three ballot fights, a boulevard replaced it.
story: In the mid-1950s, city planners called Hayes Valley blighted and in need of 'social surgery'. By 1959 the elevated Central Freeway had been built through it as far as Turk Street [1]. The wealthier neighbourhoods to the north, active in the freeway revolts, blocked its extension, so the freeway emptied its traffic onto Hayes Valley's streets. By the late 1960s more than 150,000 vehicles a day came through, and by the 1970s the freeway's shadow was notorious for drug dealing and prostitution [1]. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake shut the freeway. The damaged stretch north of Fell Street was torn down, which opened Hayes Street to the sky and helped its shops revive [1]. Then came three ballot measures, in 1997, 1998 and 1999. In 1997, Proposition H, backed by west-side and merchant groups, passed with 53 percent to rebuild the freeway, shocking residents and City Hall alike [2]. The fight went on. The final compromise ended the freeway just south of Market Street and replaced the rest with a tree-lined boulevard along Octavia. It opened after an 11 a.m. ribbon-cutting at Octavia and Market on September 9, 2005 [3]. 'Half the city wanted the freeway restored, and half wanted it torn down,' a Caltrans spokesman said [3].

title: From cactus-shop café to Zuni
hook: Zuni began in a corner of a cactus shop, cooking on an espresso machine, a toaster oven and a Weber grill. Its roast chicken became famous.
story: In 1979 Billy West opened a little café in one corner of a triangular building on Market Street. Most of the building belonged to a cactus shop called Red Desert, and the café borrowed its Southwestern style. West cooked Southwest food with an espresso machine, a toaster oven and a Weber grill [1]. Through the 1980s he expanded it, made it a queer hot spot, and won praise from the British food writer Elizabeth David [1]. In 1987 he brought in Chez Panisse alumna Judy Rodgers as chef and partner [1]. As a teenage exchange student in France, Rodgers had lived with the Troisgros family, whose restaurant had three Michelin stars [2]. She insisted on a massive wood-fired brick oven long before other chefs took up the idea. From it came a roast chicken with bread salad that became the signature dish, alongside a benchmark Caesar salad [2][1]. Zuni won the James Beard Foundation's top restaurant award in 2003, and Rodgers won its chef's award a year later [2]. West died in 1994 of complications related to AIDS, and Rodgers died in 2013 [1]. When a new chef later took over the kitchen, some dishes, the chicken among them, could not be changed [1].

title: A Castro's house joins the gay center

place.label: Fallon Building and SF LGBT Center, 1800 Market Street

hook: The founders of San Francisco's gay community center planned to demolish an 1894 Victorian. Gay preservationists fought back. The house had been built by a member of the Castro family.
story: The Victorian at Market and Octavia was built in 1894 by Carmel Fallon, born into the prominent Californio Castro family [1]. She had married Thomas Fallon, a Bear Flag Revolt veteran and later mayor of San Jose. According to the landmark account, she caught him with the maid, divorced him, and invested her settlement in San Francisco real estate [1]. Her building is the only survivor of its row on this stretch of Market. The 1906 fire took the buildings to its east, and development later took those to the west [1]. In December 1996, leaders of a proposed gay and lesbian community center bought the site. In 1997 their board voted 'not to use' the battered house after the architects estimated that renovating it would cost $1.6 to $2.6 million [2]. A coalition of gay activists and preservationists rallied to save it and collected more than 1,000 signatures [2]. The Chronicle pointed out the irony: a gay center was about to demolish a house built by a Castro, a name that had come to symbolize the gay movement around the world [2]. The house survived. It became city Landmark No. 223, and it is now part of the San Francisco LGBT Community Center, which opened in March 2002 [1][3].

title: Jazz finally gets a home
hook: After thirty years of trucking pianos to borrowed stages, SFJAZZ opened a hall of its own, billed as the first freestanding building in the West made for jazz.
story: SFJAZZ has produced the San Francisco Jazz Festival since 1983 [2]. For three decades it rented trucks to deliver pianos and drums to gigs at other people's venues [1]. In January 2013 it opened a home of its own at Fell and Franklin, billed as the first freestanding building in the West built for jazz performance and education. More than $60 million had been raised over more than a decade to build it [1]. McCoy Tyner, Chick Corea and Esperanza Spalding played the opening gala on a rainy night, with Tom Waits and Amy Tan in the audience [1]. Architect Mark Cavagnero's $64 million building has a see-through glass ground floor. Above it, bands of clear and translucent glass deliberately fail to line up from one floor to the next, an 'off-center syncopation', in the words of Chronicle critic John King [3]. Inside, the 700-seat auditorium wraps seats all the way around the stage. 'I didn't want anything axial, where you feel like you should be in the middle,' Cavagnero said [3]. News coverage of the opening linked the hall to the Fillmore a few blocks north. The Fillmore was once nicknamed 'Harlem of the West', and many of its jazz clubs were destroyed by urban renewal [1].

title: Coming home at 55 Laguna

place.label: Openhouse at 55 Laguna Street (former Richardson Hall)

hook: An old teachers' college campus became the nation's largest LGBTQ+-welcoming affordable housing for seniors.
story: Richardson Hall was built at 55 Laguna in 1925 as the Kindergarten Training Building of the San Francisco State Teachers College. It is one of three city landmarks on a campus listed on the National Register [1]. After the college left, the University of California Extension used the site until the mid-2000s [2]. More than 20 years before that, two women had begun worrying about where the city's LGBTQ+ elders would live. They were Dr. Marcy Adelman and Jeanette Gurevitch, the founders of Openhouse [3]. Working with Mercy Housing, Openhouse won a landmark decision from the Planning Commission in 2012 for what it describes as the nation's largest LGBTQ+-welcoming low-income housing project [3]. Residents began moving into the renovated 55 Laguna in December 2016. That same year Openhouse opened San Francisco's first LGBTQ+ senior center next door at 65 Laguna [3]. In 2019 residents moved into a new building at 95 Laguna, named for the two founders [3]. Of the 117 apartments, 14 are reserved for formerly homeless people through the federal Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS program. Historic murals are preserved throughout the buildings [3].
